props.title: Elvis

sections.content: Baz Luhrmann's **Elvis (2022)** (2022) explodes onto the screen with the director's signature maximalist style, joining a rich lineage of musical biopics that revolutionized the genre. Like **Bohemian Rhapsody** (2018) and **Rocketman** (2019), it transcends simple biography to capture cultural revolution. Austin Butler's transformative performance channels Presley's raw magnetism, while Tom Hanks' Colonel Tom Parker provides the Mephistophelean narrator driving this uniquely American tragedy. The film's frenetic editing and split-screens echo Elvis's own explosive impact on 1950s society.

sections.content: Luhrmann's maximalist approach mirrors earlier groundbreaking music biopics like **Amadeus** (1984) and **All That Jazz** (1979), films that broke from traditional biography to capture their subjects' artistic spirit. The movie's structure - told through Colonel Parker's unreliable narration - creates a carnival mirror reflection of Elvis's life, much like **I, Tonya** (2017) used multiple perspectives to deconstruct truth and myth. The film's portrayal of Elvis's relationship with Black music and culture also connects to deeper conversations raised in films like **Ma Rainey's Black Bottom** (2020).

The film's exploration of fame's toxicity recalls **La Vie en Rose** (2007) and **Judy** (2019), showing how the machinery of stardom both creates and destroys its subjects. Butler's performance captures Elvis's transformation from truck driver to icon, while never losing sight of the human beneath the jumpsuit. The Vegas sequences particularly echo the tragic grandeur of **A Star Is Born** (2018), showing an artist trapped by their own success. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Music Biopics

sections.content: **Elvis** represents a new wave of music biopics that prioritize visceral experience over strict historical accuracy. Like **Get On Up** (2014) and **Miles Ahead** (2015), it uses nonlinear storytelling and stylistic flourishes to capture its subject's artistic essence. The film's treatment of Elvis's cultural appropriation controversy shows how contemporary biopics are more willing to engage with complex historical questions, similar to how **Selena** (1997) addressed issues of identity and culture.
